newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace to fight on despite oil licence snub.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace to fight on despite oil licence snub.

text.p: Environmental group Greenpeace said on Monday it would continue its campaign to block oil developments in Atlantic waters off the northern Scottish coast, despite losing out to international oil companies in its bid for acreage in Britain's latest licensing round.

"The Government is acting in the interests of the oil industry and against the interests of our children. The oil industry should get its snout out of the Rockall Trough," said Greenpeace Deputy Executive director Chris Rose.

The successful bidders were 14 oil companies -- including international giants Shell and Texaco -- which were awarded permits in the 17th offshore licensing round to explore for oil mainly in the Rockall Trough west of the Hebrides and north of the Shetland islands, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said on Monday.
"This is a disastrous decision for the environment taken without parliamentary or public consultation and under cover of election fever," said Greenpeace campaigner Matthew Spencer.
Greenpeace bid for all of the 22,000 square miles of unexplored seabed on offer in the hope of turning it into a marine wildlife sanctuary.

"One organisation applied to undertake work that does not require a petroleum production licence...This did not represent a valid application and its application fee is being returned," the DTI said in a statement.

Greenpeace last week made a complaint to the European Commission claiming that the licensing process flouts European law because environmental assessments required under a 1985 European Union directive were not carried out.
"We will be pursuing our complaint to the Commission and we will also be asking the European Parliament to take up the issue," said Greenpeace's Spencer.
